name: HEPTA-X activity targeting DPRK IT workers

attribution.legal_posture: Gordon assesses with low confidence that HEPTA-X may itself be North Korean activity spying on DPRK IT workers. Generic TTPs, weak operational security, and imperfect exclusions of other actors limit confidence

ttps: Add the created account to Remote Desktop permissions
Connect to actor infrastructure through AstrillVPN
Create a local administrative account with a weak reused password
Enable RDP for persistent remote access
Exclude System32 from Windows Defender scanning
Retrieve a second-stage payload from shared command-and-control infrastructure
Trojanize software likely to be downloaded specifically by DPRK IT workers
Use open directories and shared infrastructure that permit campaign pivoting
caveats: HEPTA-X remains an unconfirmed DPRK attribution.
The reported exposure stays within the cited source boundary; a natural-person identity requires additional evidence.
The talk explicitly rules out several alternatives only imperfectly and keeps attribution at low confidence.
This is an actor/cluster lead; worker-persona status requires separate evidence.

infrastructure.value: Namecheap-linked/adversary-registered infrastructure and open directories described in talk
Backdoored installers for Hotmon, IP Messenger, Google Update, and WinRAR-like software
QuasarRAT, ChromePass, zipped LNK/PowerShell lures, RDP enablement

sources.support: Official conference-channel recording of Daniel Gordon’s research into backdoored software distributed to DPRK IT workers and a low-confidence attribution assessment for the HEPTA-X cluster
sources.locator: 01:45–09:31 Hopana Tech/Hotmon findings; 09:31–18:55 HEPTA-X investigation and attribution; 18:55–20:23 takeaways
